# File-Type Filtering in ripgrep

ripgrep comes with built-in support for searching specific file types. Instead of memorizing file extensions or writing glob patterns every time you search, you can use simple type names to limit your search to the files you care about.

## What Are File Types?

ripgrep organizes files into *types*. Each type is a name that represents one or more file patterns. For example, the `rust` type includes all files ending in `.rs`. The `c` type includes C source files (`.c`, `.h`, `.h.in`) and other C-related patterns. ripgrep ships with over a hundred pre-defined types covering common programming languages, markup formats, configuration formats, archives, and more.

## Finding Available Types: `--type-list`

To see all available file types and what files they match, use the `--type-list` flag:

```
$ rg --type-list
ada: *.adb, *.ads
agda: *.agda, *.lagda
asm: *.asm, *.s, *.S
c: *.[chH], *.[chH].in, *.cats
cpp: *.[ChH], *.cc, *.[ch]pp, *.[ch]xx, *.hh, *.inl, ...
go: *.go
json: *.json
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
python: *.py, *.pyi
rust: *.rs
shell: *.bash, *.ksh, *.sh, *.zsh, ...
toml: *.toml
```

Each line shows a type name, a colon, and then the patterns (file extensions and specific filenames) that belong to that type. This is a read-only listing—it shows you what ripgrep already knows about.

## Searching Only One Type: `--type`

To limit a search to files of a particular type, use the `--type` flag followed by the type name. For example, to search only in Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

This is equivalent to searching with the glob pattern `*.rs`, but shorter and easier to remember. You can also use the short form `-t`:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The short form combines the flag and type into a single argument. You can chain multiple type flags together if you want to search multiple types at once:

```
$ rg 'TODO' -tpython -tshell -ttmpl
```

This searches in Python files, shell scripts, and template files all in the same search.

The type name must be recognized by ripgrep or previously added with `--type-add` (see below). If you try to use a type that doesn't exist, ripgrep will report an error.

### The Special `all` Type

`--type all` is a convenience that searches across all file types that ripgrep recognizes. This puts ripgrep into "whitelist" mode—it will only search files whose types ripgrep knows about, skipping unknown files. This is useful when you want to be thorough but skip binary files and other unrecognized content.

## Excluding Types: `--type-not`

The opposite of `--type` is `--type-not`, which excludes files of a given type from the search. For example, to search everywhere except in Python files:

```
$ rg 'import' --type-not python
```

Or use the short form with a capital T:

```
$ rg 'import' -Tpython
```

You can combine multiple exclusions:

```
$ rg 'print' -Tpython -Tshell
```

This searches everywhere except Python and shell scripts.

### The Special `all` Type with `--type-not`

`--type-not all` puts ripgrep into "blacklist" mode—it will only search files whose types ripgrep *doesn't* recognize. This finds unidentified files and lets you search in content that isn't part of any known type.

## Creating Custom Types: `--type-add`

If ripgrep doesn't have a type for what you're searching, you can create your own. The `--type-add` flag lets you define a new type by specifying glob patterns:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb 'title'
```

This creates a new type called `web` that matches HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, then searches for `title` only in those files. You can also use glob expansion to add multiple patterns at once:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb 'title'
```

When you run `--type-list` after defining a custom type, it will appear in the output.

### Important: Custom Types Don't Persist

Custom types defined with `--type-add` only apply to the current command. When you run ripgrep again, the custom type is gone. If you want a custom type available every time you search, save it to ripgrep's configuration file. Create or edit `~/.ripgreprc` (or the path specified by your `RIPGREP_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable) and add the definition:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

Then it will be available in every ripgrep invocation without needing to pass `--type-add` on the command line.

## Combining File-Type Filters with Other Filtering

File-type filters work alongside ripgrep's other filtering mechanisms:

- Glob patterns (`-g` flag) take precedence over type definitions. If you specify `-g '*.rs' -Tpython`, glob wins.
- Ignore files (like `.gitignore`) can override type filters as well.
- By default, ripgrep still respects gitignore rules even when you use `--type`. To search without gitignore rules, use the `--no-ignore` flag.

## Common Patterns

**Search multiple types:** `rg 'pattern' -tpython -tgo -tshell`

**Search everything except one type:** `rg 'pattern' --type-not node_modules`

**Create a composite type:** `rg --type-add 'backend:*.go' --type-add 'backend:*.rs' -tbackend 'error'`

**Search only recognized files:** `rg 'pattern' --type all`

**Search only unrecognized files:** `rg 'pattern' --type-not all`

## Precedence and Behavior

- Multiple `--type` flags combine additively: use them together to search multiple types.
- Multiple `--type-not` flags combine additively: each one adds to the exclusion list.
- You can mix `--type` and `--type-not`, and ripgrep will respect both: search only files that match at least one type flag AND exclude any that match at least one type-not flag.
- Type filters have lower precedence than glob patterns and ignore-file rules, so those can override type-based filtering if needed.
